name: Daniel Fitzgerald
presenting_complaint: Fever and rigors 10 days after chemotherapy, feeling generally unwell

conditions: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma on R-CHOP chemotherapy (day 10 of cycle 2)
medical_history.social: Non-smoker, minimal alcohol. Lives with wife, works as an accountant (currently on leave).

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 54-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma presents to ED with fever to 38.8C and rigors, 10 days after his second cycle of R-CHOP chemotherapy. He has a PICC line in situ and looks flushed and unwell. Obs: BP 98/58, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 95% on room air, temp 38.8C, GCS 15. This is febrile neutropenia until proven otherwise and is a medical emergency.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Confirm chemotherapy details: regimen (R-CHOP), day of cycle (day 10 — nadir period), and that this is a fever in a likely neutropenic patient
State explicitly that this is febrile neutropenia and a medical emergency requiring antibiotics within 1 hour
Source screen by history: mouth/throat pain, cough/dyspnoea, dysuria, abdominal pain/diarrhoea, PICC line site symptoms, skin/perineal pain
Rigors, quantified fever, and any hypotension/altered conscious state suggesting sepsis or septic shock
Medication and allergy history documented (penicillin allergy status directly changes empirical antibiotic choice)
objective: Take blood cultures from a PERIPHERAL site AND from every lumen of the central line/PICC before antibiotics — but do not let cultures delay the first antibiotic dose beyond 1 hour
Full septic examination: mouth, chest, abdomen, skin, PICC line exit site and perineum (inspect only — NO digital rectal examination in a neutropenic patient)
Full obs and sepsis assessment: BP 98/58 and HR 122 indicate haemodynamic compromise — reassess after fluids
Bedside VBG with lactate, and place patient in isolation with neutropenic precautions
Chest X-ray and urinalysis to look for a source
assessment: Febrile neutropenia with sepsis (hypotensive, tachycardic) — a haematological emergency; do not wait for the neutrophil count to confirm before treating
Consider line-associated sepsis given PICC in situ; consider septic shock requiring ICU
Differentials for the source: chest, urinary, gut/mucositis, skin/perineal, and central-line infection
plan: Antibiotics within 1 HOUR is the make-or-break action: give piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV immediately (per eTG); if immediate/severe penicillin allergy use cefepime 2 g IV or meropenem 1 g IV
Do NOT wait for the FBC/neutrophil count or other investigations before giving the first antibiotic dose
Blood cultures from peripheral site and every lumen of the PICC BEFORE antibiotics, but never delaying antibiotics beyond 1 hour
Add vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg IV loading dose if line infection, haemodynamic instability, or MRSA risk suspected
IV fluid resuscitation (e.g. 500 mL-1 L crystalloid bolus) for hypotension, reassess and repeat; escalate to ICU if shock persists
Bloods: FBC (confirms neutropenia), UEC, LFT, CRP, lactate, coags, cultures from all sites; CXR and urinalysis
Isolation with neutropenic precautions and strict hand hygiene; document a clear examination excluding a DRE
Urgent referral: call the haematology/oncology registrar and ED consultant early; ICU review given sepsis

critical_errors: Delaying antibiotics beyond 1 hour by waiting for the neutrophil count or other investigation results — antibiotics must be given empirically within the hour
Performing a digital rectal examination in a neutropenic patient (risk of bacteraemia and mucosal injury)
must_not_miss: Febrile neutropenia recognised as an emergency and empirical antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV) given within 1 hour
Sepsis/septic shock recognised and treated with fluids and early ICU escalation
Blood cultures from peripheral site and every central-line lumen taken before antibiotics
Central-line-associated infection considered as the source
